body:
I was intrigued by the high rating, based upon the pretty good-sized voting sample, and the apparent role Roger Corman played as a producer. And there is also the fact that this was a product of mainland China, not Taiwan.

The verdict? While it is not a bad film by any fair assessment, I do not think this is a 7.2.

POTD is a story, respectively, of the Chinese direction of a horror movie and the contemporaneous American direction of a documentary. Both films are addressing the same subject: the imperial-age murder of a Chinese courtesan by her rival, and the determination of the deceased woman to exact revenge on her rival. However, the two narratives part ways from there.

The Chinese language portion is largely concerned with an actress in the production who has come to identify with the deceased woman she plays. She has done so to the point where her dreams are full of death, ghostly images and hatred for her own worldly rivals. The director and his assistants are unsure what to do about this over-identification with the role.

The English language portion concerns a team of documentary film makers, headed by "Rebecca" and her producer. The team is attempting to document the particulars of a Chinese ghost festival.

However, despite this seemingly equal framing of the Chinese and English-language portions of the film, the American (English) portion of the film accounts for roughly 75% of the running time.

The print quality and special effects were actually quite good. The problems seem to stem from the writing and editing, which tended to be quite rough. Moreover, a number of different characters are introduced with little to no backstory, leaving the viewer to piece together who they are and what they are doing in the film. Finally, some key narrative elements are introduced and then just dropped. For example, we learn that Rebecca lost her co-director and fiance, David, to an untimely death. Early on, there is a discussion of ghost marriages in death, an interesting idea that would seem tailored for the script. However, after broaching this issue, the film basically drops it (and David), never to be revisited again.

POTD does feel like it was designed to remind viewers of something like Corman's Edgar Allen Poe films or "The Tomb of Ligeia (1964)." However, while POTD is certainly suitable, it lacks the professional edits, dialogue and temperament of those films.
This film-in-film takes excerpts from Palace of the Damned where Yixin Li played the ghost.
